leading_positions.synthesis: All six round 1 files explicitly place Mircea Cărtărescu (B006) as the sole preferred laureate, with a single prize part and a single credited name. Shared grounds are a distinctive voice, dense patterned prose that joins memory, the body, dream and cosmology, and an architecture that members describe as cumulative across Blinding (the first volume of the Orbitor trilogy) and Solenoid. Each member also states the main reservation: the claim depends on Romanian sentence rhythm and density, which translation may flatten, and none has read the originals. What is not shared is the citation scope. Carlberg's citation names a prose and poetic oeuvre. Palm and Sem-Sandberg would centre the prose project and treat the poetry as origin or context. Sward and Palm want the citation to name the cumulative architecture and not only the imagery. Members also differ on whether the later long works deepen or restate the early motifs, and the files leave that question open. All six name Adonis (B005) as an alternative. Beyond that, the listed alternatives differ: B027 (Zurita) for Carlberg, Olsson and Sem-Sandberg, B018 (Michon) for Mattson, B042 (Carson) for Palm, and B035 (Can Xue) for Sward. These alternatives are not preferred configurations.

areas_of_agreement: All six members prefer a single-laureate configuration naming only Mircea Cărtărescu, and each says the preference rests on the common literary criteria and not on the opening rankings, fame, age or national symbolism.

Every member names translation dependence as the main risk to the Cărtărescu case. They also agree that poetry and early fiction are unevenly translated, so the whole-oeuvre claim leans on the major novels.
Every member says they have not read the works and cannot independently verify them. Judgments rest on public knowledge and colleagues' descriptions.

Adonis (B005) is the named alternative of all six members. Members consistently say his case should rest on the poems and not on his essays or public commentary. They also say his age is not a literary criterion.
Members agree that any Zurita citation should be anchored in the page-based poetic sequences, with the landscape and sky works treated as extensions of the poetry.
Members agree that cross-genre work such as Carson's is hard to compare with novel-centred oeuvres under common criteria. They treat this as a reason for caution, not dismissal.
Members treat Michon's sentence-level concentration as a real linguistic achievement, and do not treat a compact corpus as disqualifying in itself.
scientific_disputes: There is no explicit dispute over who is preferred. The open questions concern how far the case for Cărtărescu can be assessed through translation, and how confidently Romanian density and rhythm can be credited without original-language expert input.

Members differ on how much the Adonis case is exposed to translation loss. Carlberg, Sem-Sandberg, Olsson and Palm rank him behind Cărtărescu partly because Arabic prosody and intertextual form are harder for the committee to verify. Mattson calls him a very close second. Whether this is a difference in evidence or in merit is not settled.

Carson: Palm sees formal invention carrying emotional and intellectual weight. Sem-Sandberg, Olsson and Carlberg question whether some hybridity is gesture, and whether the book-object works (such as Nox) survive translation.

Zurita: members disagree about how far the landscape and sky works can be assessed as literature, and whether the later collections sustain the early sequences. No member claims to have settled either point.
Michon: Mattson rates the compression and formal precision highly. Most others accept the quality but ask whether intensity can substitute for range in a prize for the whole body of work.
Whether the maximalist, recursive method of Cărtărescu's long books amounts to sustained quality or to length alone is raised as an open question by Sem-Sandberg, Sward and Olsson.
attribution_disputes: No dispute exists over the laureate's identity: every file names Mircea Cărtărescu alone, and no organization, translator or additional name is proposed.

The citation scope differs. Carlberg's wording includes poetic work. Palm and Sem-Sandberg would centre the prose or novelistic project and treat the poetry as origin or context, because poetry coverage in translation is thinnest. Sward and Palm want the citation to name the formal architecture and not only the visionary imagery.

If Adonis were chosen, members differ on how much the essays should appear in the citation. Mattson would name them only as part of the same project, and Carlberg and Sem-Sandberg would keep the verse central.
If Carson were chosen, it is unresolved whether the citation would rest on poetry, essay or translation. If Zurita were chosen, it is unresolved whether the non-textual works belong in the citation.
maturity_disputes: Whether Cărtărescu's later work deepens or repeats the motifs of the Orbitor trilogy and Solenoid is uncertain. Palm reads an escalation of scale and structure but marks it as a judgment from public knowledge. Sward, Sem-Sandberg, Carlberg and Olsson treat it as an open question.
Whether the poetry and early fiction sustain the level of the major novels is unestablished, because of uneven translation coverage.
Michon: Mattson and Sem-Sandberg acknowledge the weight a slim corpus puts on the breadth criterion. Several members say they would reconsider if intensity were accepted as a substitute for breadth.

Other candidates also carry maturity questions: Murnane's restricted range, Carson's smaller conventional corpus, Can Xue's sustained quality across similar-seeming work, and whether Zurita's later collections hold the early level.
conflict_or_recusal_flags: Carlberg's actual committee voting status is undocumented, and her simulated vote is a modeling assumption, as her own file also states.

Carlberg's file discloses that she was elected to the Academy alongside Sem-Sandberg in 2020 and is married to a former finance minister. She sees no connection to any shortlisted writer and asserts no recusal. This is recorded from her file and not independently verified.
Sem-Sandberg's file notes Central European subject matter and long residence in Prague and Vienna. It records no tie to Cărtărescu or any other shortlisted writer.
Olsson (chair and a voting member) records his scholarly work on Celan, the fragment, exile literature and modern poetry as context only, with no personal or professional tie to a shortlisted writer.

Palm's and Sward's own writing practices are noted by those members as context and not as evidence of preference. No recusal is asserted in any file, and conflicts are disclosed here but not adjudicated.
questions_for_round2: Which specific passages or volumes of the Orbitor trilogy and Solenoid should the committee rely on to decide whether the later work deepens or restates the early motifs, and does any member's view change if it does only the latter?

Should the Cărtărescu citation name the prose and its architecture alone (Palm, Sem-Sandberg), or the whole poetic and prose oeuvre (Carlberg), and what justifies including the poetry given its thin translation coverage?
What translation or original-language evidence on the Romanian prose would let members move from a provisional to a firm preference, and would unavailable expert input change anyone's ranking?

Several members rank Adonis behind Cărtărescu mainly because Arabic prosody is harder to verify. Is that a difference in the strength of the claim or only in the evidence available to the committee, and what would justify placing Adonis first or equal?
Where should the committee draw the line between concentration and breadth for Michon: is there a stated standard under which a compact oeuvre supports a whole-oeuvre citation?
Is any member prepared to specify which works, and what citation scope, would make Carson or Zurita a first choice, as Carlberg offered for Carson?
Does any member hold a reservation about Cărtărescu strong enough to prevent a vote for him, and if so what is it?
summary.chair_observation: All six round 1 files prefer B006 and name B005 as an alternative. Agreement on a single laureate is not evidence of merit, and the files themselves say so. The reservations are shared and concern evidence, not preference: translation loss, uneven coverage of the poetry, and uncertainty about whether the later long works deepen the project or restate it. Round 2 should therefore test the Cărtărescu case against these specific uncertainties and settle the citation scope before any comparison of alternatives. Some round 1 responses refer to writers who are not on this shortlist (for example Kincaid and Wright), and these are set aside here. This summary counts only positions explicit in the six files and makes no claim about confidential proceedings or the full Academy's decision.
